Empirical Bayes Disease Mapping in Pennsylvania

Lung cancer: global and local smoothing

Author

Eric M. Delmelle · Lehigh University · BSTA 374

Today’s goals

We will use lung cancer counts in Pennsylvania’s 67 counties (2002). You already know how to calculate a standardized incidence ratio (SIR). Today we focus on smoothing those SIRs with two methods: global empirical Bayes (EB) and local empirical Bayes (local EB).

By the end, you should be able to:

  1. explain why a county with few expected cases can have an extreme SIR;
  2. explain the weighted average used by empirical Bayes;
  3. distinguish borrowing from the state and borrowing from neighbors;
  4. interpret the three maps: raw SIR, global EB, and local EB.
Note

Install the required packages once. The lung cancer data are already included in SpatialEpi—no shapefile or CSV download is needed.

Code 
install.packages(c("sf", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "spdep", "SpatialEpi"))
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(spdep)
library(SpatialEpi)

1. A quick reminder: raw SIRs

Prepare the lung cancer data

The dataset has 16 records per county, corresponding to combinations of race, sex, and age. To obtain an age-, sex-, and race-standardized SIR, we first calculate Pennsylvania’s rate within each group (stratum).

\[ E_i = \sum_s P_{is} r_s, \qquad \mathrm{SIR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i}. \]

Here, \(O_i\) = observed cases, \(E_i\) = expected cases, \(P_{is}\) = county population in stratum \(s\), and \(r_s\) = Pennsylvania rate in that stratum. SIR = 1 means the observed count equals the expected count.

data("pennLC_sf", package = "SpatialEpi")

# The original sf object contains 16 records per county.
d <- pennLC_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry()

# Reference rate for every race / sex / age stratum.
reference <- d |>
  group_by(race, gender, age) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(cases) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")

# One record per county: observed cases, expected cases, and SIR.
county_data <- d |>
  left_join(reference, by = c("race", "gender", "age")) |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(O = sum(cases), E = sum(population * rate), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(county = as.character(county), SIR = O / E)

# Keep one polygon per county and attach our calculations.
pa <- pennLC_sf |>
  group_by(county) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(county) |>
  mutate(county = as.character(county)) |>
  left_join(county_data, by = "county") |>
  arrange(county)

stopifnot(nrow(pa) == 67, !anyNA(pa$O), all(pa$E > 0))

pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(counties = n(), observed_cases = sum(O),
            expected_cases = round(sum(E)))
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  counties observed_cases expected_cases
     <int>          <int>          <dbl>
1       67          10279          10279

Look at the raw SIRs

Code 
# Fixed breaks will be reused for all three maps.
risk_breaks <- c(0, 0.67, 0.83, 0.95, 1.05, 1.20, 1.50, Inf)
risk_labels <- c("<0.67", "0.67–0.83", "0.83–0.95", "0.95–1.05",
                 "1.05–1.20", "1.20–1.50", ">1.50")

risk_class <- function(x) {
  cut(x, breaks = risk_breaks, labels = risk_labels,
      include.lowest = TRUE)
}

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = risk_class(SIR)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1,
                    drop = FALSE, name = "SIR") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))

Consider the counties with the lowest and highest SIRs. Look not only at the SIR but also at E, the expected number of cases.

Code 
county_data |>
  arrange(SIR) |>
  slice(c(1:3, (n() - 2):n())) |>
  mutate(E = round(E, 1), SIR = round(SIR, 2))
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  county       O     E   SIR
  <chr>    <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 juniata      6  18.7  0.32
2 sullivan     3   7.4  0.4 
3 montour      8  16.1  0.5 
4 cameron      8   5.9  1.35
5 venango     70  51.1  1.37
6 potter      22  16    1.37

An SIR can change dramatically when a county has only a small number of expected cases. Empirical Bayes reduces the influence of such extreme raw values.

2. Global empirical Bayes: borrow from Pennsylvania

One simple formula

A global empirical Bayes estimate is a weighted average of the county’s raw SIR and the overall Pennsylvania reference:

\[ \widehat\theta_i = w_i\,\mathrm{SIR}_i + (1-w_i)\,m, \qquad w_i = \frac{a}{a + m/E_i}. \]

  • \(m\): overall reference (approximately 1 because the expected counts were calculated using Pennsylvania rates);
  • \(a\): estimated between-county variation;
  • \(w_i\): weight placed on the county’s own SIR, between 0 and 1.

When \(E_i\) is small, \(w_i\) tends to be smaller and the county’s SIR moves more toward the statewide reference. The data determine \(a\) and \(m\); we do not choose arbitrary weights.

Run global empirical Bayes

# Counts (O) and expected cases (E) give smoothed relative risks.
eb_global <- EBest(pa$O, pa$E, family = "poisson")
pa$RR_global <- eb_global$estmm

# In the Poisson implementation, parameters are called 'a' and 'b'.
# 'b' is the overall reference m; 'a' is between-county variation.
par_global <- attr(eb_global, "parameters")
a_global <- par_global$a
m_global <- par_global$b

# Weight on the county's observed SIR.
pa$w_global <- a_global / (a_global + m_global / pa$E)

# Confirm the weighted-average formula reproduces EBest() results.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  unname(pa$RR_global),
  unname(pa$w_global * pa$SIR + (1 - pa$w_global) * m_global),
  tolerance = 1e-7
)))

c(state_reference = m_global, between_county_variation = a_global)
         state_reference between_county_variation 
              1.00000000               0.00926715
Code 
pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "venango",
                       "lehigh", "philadelphia")) |>
  arrange(E) |>
  transmute(county, O, expected = round(E, 1),
            raw_SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            weight = round(w_global, 2),
            global_EB = round(RR_global, 2))
# A tibble: 5 × 6
  county           O expected raw_SIR weight global_EB
  <chr>        <int>    <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 sullivan         3      7.4    0.4    0.06      0.96
2 potter          22     16      1.37   0.13      1.05
3 venango         70     51.1    1.37   0.32      1.12
4 lehigh         252    260.     0.97   0.71      0.98
5 philadelphia  1415   1219.     1.16   0.92      1.15

A weight near 1 preserves most of the original SIR. A weight near 0 means more borrowing from the statewide reference.

Code 
ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = w_global), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), name = "Weight on SIR") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)

Question: Which counties retain more of their own SIR—the large or small counties? Why?

3. Local empirical Bayes: borrow from neighbors

Define the neighbors

Instead of one statewide reference, local EB uses a different neighborhood reference for each county. We begin with queen contiguity: counties are neighbors when they share part of a boundary or a corner.

nb <- poly2nb(pa, queen = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(nb) == nrow(pa), all(card(nb) > 0))

# Inspect the neighbors of Lehigh County.
i <- match("lehigh", pa$county)
pa$county[nb[[i]]]
[1] "berks"       "bucks"       "carbon"      "montgomery"  "northampton"
[6] "schuylkill"
Code 
pa$neighbor_group <- "Other counties"
pa$neighbor_group[nb[[i]]] <- "Lehigh's neighbors"
pa$neighbor_group[i] <- "Lehigh"

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = neighbor_group), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Lehigh" = "#b2182b",
                               "Lehigh's neighbors" = "#92c5de",
                               "Other counties" = "grey92"),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Run local empirical Bayes

# Local EB uses neighbors' counts and expected cases.
eb_local <- EBlocal(pa$O, pa$E, nb,
                    zero.policy = FALSE, spChk = FALSE)
pa$RR_local <- eb_local$est

# Each county has its own local reference and its own smoothing weight.
par_local <- attr(eb_local, "parameters")
pa$m_local <- par_local$m
pa$w_local <- par_local$a /
  (par_local$a + par_local$m / pa$E)

stopifnot(all(is.finite(pa$RR_local)))

Local EB follows the same idea as global EB, but replaces the statewide reference with a neighborhood reference. For this function, that reference is calculated from the neighboring counties (not the focal county). The local reference and weight may differ substantially from place to place.

Code 
pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "venango",
                       "lehigh", "philadelphia")) |>
  arrange(E) |>
  transmute(county, expected = round(E, 1),
            raw_SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            neighbor_reference = round(m_local, 2),
            local_weight = round(w_local, 2),
            local_EB = round(RR_local, 2))
# A tibble: 5 × 6
  county       expected raw_SIR neighbor_reference local_weight local_EB
  <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>              <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1 sullivan          7.4    0.4                0.95         0.01     0.94
2 potter           16      1.37               0.94         0.06     0.97
3 venango          51.1    1.37               1.04         0.32     1.15
4 lehigh          260.     0.97               1            0.21     0.99
5 philadelphia   1219.     1.16               1.09         0.72     1.14

For example, Lehigh County has the following values:

Code 
pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(county == "lehigh") |>
  transmute(county,
            SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            state_reference = round(m_global, 2),
            neighbor_reference = round(m_local, 2),
            global_EB = round(RR_global, 2),
            local_EB = round(RR_local, 2))
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  county   SIR state_reference neighbor_reference global_EB local_EB
  <chr>  <dbl>           <dbl>              <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 lehigh  0.97               1                  1      0.98     0.99

Question: Why is the local EB estimate not necessarily closer to 1 than the raw SIR? Think about the risk in the neighboring counties.

4. Compare all three maps

Code 
pa |>
  select(county, SIR, RR_global, RR_local) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SIR, RR_global, RR_local),
               names_to = "method", values_to = "risk") |>
  mutate(method = factor(method,
                         levels = c("SIR", "RR_global", "RR_local"),
                         labels = c("Raw SIR", "Global EB", "Local EB"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = risk_class(risk)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ method, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1,
                    drop = FALSE, name = "Relative risk") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))

Let’s also look at the counties whose estimated risk changes the most.

Code 
pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(change_global = abs(RR_global - SIR),
         change_local = abs(RR_local - SIR)) |>
  arrange(desc(change_global)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  transmute(county, expected = round(E),
            SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            global_EB = round(RR_global, 2),
            local_EB = round(RR_local, 2),
            global_change = round(change_global, 2))
# A tibble: 8 × 6
  county   expected   SIR global_EB local_EB global_change
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>
1 juniata        19  0.32      0.9      0.73          0.58
2 sullivan        7  0.4       0.96     0.94          0.56
3 montour        16  0.5       0.93     0.92          0.44
4 cameron         6  1.35      1.02     0.98          0.33
5 potter         16  1.37      1.05     0.97          0.33
6 wyoming        21  0.67      0.95     0.91          0.28
7 venango        51  1.37      1.12     1.15          0.25
8 forest          5  0.74      0.99     0.98          0.25
TipRemember

Global EB: each county borrows from the same Pennsylvania reference.

Local EB: each county borrows from its own surrounding neighbors.

Both methods produce smoothed relative risks, but they need not give the same result, and local smoothing is not automatically better than global smoothing.

5. In-class exercise: 15 minutes

Work in pairs. Use your maps and the R output, and answer in plain English.

  1. Raw versus global EB (5 minutes). Choose a county with a high raw SIR and relatively few expected cases. Report its \(O\), \(E\), SIR and global EB estimate. Did its risk estimate move toward 1? Explain why.
  2. Global versus local EB (5 minutes). For Lehigh County, report the raw SIR, global EB, local EB, and the local neighborhood reference. In one or two sentences, explain why the two smoothed estimates differ.
  3. Think spatially (5 minutes). Compare the three maps. Identify one area whose appearance changes noticeably after smoothing. Which reference—state or neighbors—would be more appropriate for the question you want to ask?

Key takeaways

  • SIR = O / E: compares observed to expected cases.
  • Global empirical Bayes: a weighted average of the county SIR and a statewide reference.
  • Local empirical Bayes: a weighted average of the county SIR and a neighborhood reference.
  • Smoothing weights: determined by the data; counties with smaller expected counts often borrow more.
  • Geography matters: changing the definition of neighbors can change a local EB map.

References

  • Marshall, R. J. (1991). Mapping disease and mortality rates using empirical Bayes estimators. Applied Statistics, 40(2), 283–294.
  • Clayton, D., & Kaldor, J. (1987). Empirical Bayes estimates of age-standardized relative risks for use in disease mapping. Biometrics, 43(3), 671–681.
  • Dataset: SpatialEpi::pennLC_sf (Pennsylvania lung cancer, 2002).
  • R documentation: spdep global EB and spdep local EB.
